analysis.one_liner: Lets the government tap overseas targets' communications without individual warrants, compelling phone companies to assist.
analysis.headline: It became law in five days, passing the Senate 60-28 and the House 227-183, with a 180-day sunset but no end date for the surveillance it authorized.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill rewrote the 1978 foreign-surveillance law so that tapping the communications of a person 'reasonably believed' to be outside the United States no longer counts as 'electronic surveillance' requiring a warrant from the special foreign-intelligence court. Instead, the Attorney General and the Director of National Intelligence can authorize interception themselves for up to a year at a time, and can order phone and internet companies to help, with the government paying them for it. The new provisions expire after 180 days, but any surveillance authorization or directive issued under them keeps running until it expires on its own.
analysis.who_benefits: The executive branch's intelligence agencies gain the power to intercept international communications without getting a warrant for any specific target, and telecommunications and internet providers gain a legal shield: no lawsuit can be brought against them for complying with a government directive, and the government compensates them at the prevailing rate.

how_it_helps.text: The DNI and Attorney General may authorize interception of foreign intelligence information for up to one year based on their own written certification, rather than an individual court order for each target.

The government may direct communications providers to supply information, facilities, and assistance, and must compensate them at the prevailing rate; no cause of action lies against any person for providing that assistance.
Surveillance directed at a person reasonably believed to be outside the United States is excluded from FISA's definition of electronic surveillance, removing it from the individual-warrant process.
The Attorney General must report semiannually to the intelligence and judiciary committees on the number of certifications and directives issued and any incidents of non-compliance.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people lose warrant protection for international communications: any call or email crossing a border can be intercepted once a target is reasonably believed to be abroad, with only government-written 'minimization' procedures as the safeguard for Americans swept in. Providers' customers bear this through the compelled cooperation of their carriers, and the public learns of the program only through classified, sealed court filings and semiannual congressional reports.
analysis.who_pays_short: Anyone who calls, emails, or browses abroad

drawbacks.text: No warrant is obtained for any individual target; authorizations rest on the determination of the Attorney General and DNI, and the certification need not identify the specific facilities or places the surveillance will be directed at.

Court review is narrow: the FISA court only checks whether the government's screening procedures are 'clearly erroneous,' certifications and challenge petitions are filed under seal and reviewed ex parte, and a directive stays in effect unless a judge explicitly sets it aside.
Providers can be compelled to assist and cannot be sued for complying, so the companies that hold Americans' communications face no accountability in court for what they hand over.
Although the act terminates 180 days after enactment, every authorization and directive issued under it remains in effect until its own expiration, so the surveillance does not stop with the sunset.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — that spying on genuinely foreign targets should not require the same warrant as spying inside the United States — has a reasonable national-security rationale, and the sunset deadline plus semiannual reporting give Congress a check of sorts. But the design concentrates the authorizing power in two political appointees, keeps nearly everything sealed from the public, gives the court only a 'clearly erroneous' check on procedures rather than scrutiny of actual interceptions, and shields cooperating companies from lawsuits. Americans' cross-border communications get only the government's own written privacy procedures as protection.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on August 1, passed the Senate 60-28 on August 3, passed the House 227-183 the next day, and was signed by the President on August 5, all in the days before Congress's summer recess.

narrative.text: The Senate passed the bill with an amendment by a 60-28 vote (Record Vote 309) on August 3, 2007.
The House passed it 227-183 (Roll no. 836) on August 4, 2007, after consideration under a pre-arranged order with one hour of debate.
The President signed it on August 5, 2007, and it became Public Law 110-55.
The act's core provisions terminate 180 days after enactment, but authorizations and directives issued under the act remain in effect until they expire.
The Senate Judiciary Committee held hearings on the act on September 25, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The executive branch gained warrantless interception authority, and telecommunications providers gained compensation and immunity from suit for assisting. The 180-day sunset meant Congress had to return to the question the following year rather than leaving the expanded power in place permanently.

sides.party_line_note: Republicans backed it almost unanimously (43-0 in the Senate, 186-2 in the House); Democrats mostly opposed it but 16 Senate Democrats and 41 House Democrats joined the majority, supplying the votes that made it law.

industries.note: The bill makes communications providers the compulsory channel for government interception: they can be ordered to supply information, facilities, and assistance, are paid at the prevailing rate for it, and cannot be sued for complying. Their customers' calls and emails are what gets handed over, and the customers learn of it only through classified filings.

industries.industry: The intelligence community and executive branch
industries.note: The bill transfers the decision to intercept international communications from the foreign-intelligence court to the Attorney General and Director of National Intelligence for up to one year at a time, with court review limited to whether their procedures are 'clearly erroneous.' The gain in surveillance power comes directly at the cost of warrant protection for cross-border communications.
